title: What if a ship sailed on a sea of honey?
caption:
Ships would float higher on honey. 🍯🚢

Honey is about 40% denser than seawater (≈1.42 vs ≈1.025 g/cm³), so a hull only sinks about 72% as deep. The red underbody pokes out of the sea.

It's also thousands of times thicker than water. A 1-metre ripple that water's viscosity would take hours to calm fades in about a second.

The bonus: no barnacles. Honey's sugar pulls the water out of almost anything living.

Would this ship ever make it to port? Yes or no 👇

Send this to the friend who puts honey on everything.

Follow @the.impossible.lab for more impossible science.

⚠️ Don't try this. Deep, thick syrup can trap a person: never climb into tanks or vats of honey, molasses or syrup.

sources: https://www.fao.org/3/w0076e/w0076e04.htm (FAO, Value-added products from beekeeping, ch. 2: honey specific gravity 1.40-1.45 at 20 °C for 13-20 % water; sweet clover honey 189.6 poise = 19 Pa·s at 20.6 °C; 48-420 poise at 25 °C depending on water content)
https://berryjune07.github.io/physics/damping-of-gravity-waves.html (viscous damping of deep-water gravity waves: amplitude ~ exp(-2 nu k^2 t), valid for nu k^2 << omega)
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3609166 (Mandal & Mandal 2011: honey's high osmolarity hinders microbial growth and dehydrates bacteria)

Computed: draft ratio 1.025/1.42 = 0.72 (28 % shallower); viscosity ratio 19/0.001 ≈ 19,000 (≈5,000-20,000 across typical honeys); 1 m ripple, k = 2π/m: honey nu = 19/1420 = 0.0134 m²/s -> 1/(2 nu k²) ≈ 0.95 s (nu k² = 0.53 << omega = 7.85 rad/s); water nu = 1.0e-6 m²/s -> ≈12,700 s ≈ 3.5 h
